Pattern 23 of 24

Union-Find (Disjoint Set Union)

When things keep getting connected and you keep asking "are these two in the same group?" or "how many groups are there now?", a union-find answers both in almost constant time. It's the tool for components that only ever merge.

1. What is this pattern for?

A party where people join friend groups. Each group picks a "representative". To check whether two guests are in the same group, ask each who their representative is. When two groups meet, one representative simply starts reporting to the other. Nobody re-labels every guest; the chain of "who do you report to" does the work.

Union-find keeps a parent pointer per element. Following parents leads to the set's root, its representative.

  • find(x): follow parents to the root, shortening the path on the way (path compression).
  • union(a, b): point one root at the other (attach the smaller set under the larger: union by size).
  • Both run in amortised O(α(n)), effectively constant.

Typical uses: counting connected components as edges arrive, Kruskal's MST, merging accounts, islands appearing over time, grouping indices that can be swapped.

2. How it works (bisected)

  1. Decide what the nodes are: indices, grid cells (r · cols + c), emails, rows and columns.
  2. Initialise every node as its own root: parent[i] = i; components = n.
  3. For each connection, find both roots. If they differ, link them and decrement components.
  4. Answer queries by comparing roots, reading components, or grouping nodes by root.
  5. If connections disappear over time, process time backwards so they appear instead (union-find can't split).

3. Seeing a problem: how to spot Union-Find

Trigger words

  • "connected", "same group", "friends of friends", "belong to the same person"
  • "number of components / islands / provinces" after each operation
  • "can be swapped any number of times", "equivalent", "transitively"
  • "earliest time when everyone is connected", "last day you can still cross"
  • minimum spanning tree with an edge list (Kruskal)

Shape of the input

  • A list of pairs or edges, often arriving over time.
  • Many connectivity queries mixed with merges.
  • Brute-force smell: running BFS/DFS again after every new edge.
The one question to ask"Do groups only ever merge, and do I mostly need to know who is in the same group?"

4. When to use it, and when not to

Use union-find when…Prefer something else when…
Edges arrive one by one and you query connectivity in betweenThe graph is fixed and you query once: one DFS/BFS is simpler
You need component counts or sizes as things mergeYou need actual paths or distances: BFS / Dijkstra
Kruskal's MST, equivalence classes, swap groupsEdges get deleted: reverse time, or use another structure
Directed reachability is not neededDirection matters (dependencies): topological sort / DFS

Cost: O(α(n)) amortised per operation with path compression and union by size (α grows so slowly it's ≤ 4 for any realistic n); O(n) space.

5. The templates, step by step (Python, TypeScript, Java)

Union-Find (a disjoint-set union, DSU) keeps groups of items and answers "are these two in the same group?" in almost O(1). There's one template with two operations: find follows parent pointers to the group's root (shortening the path as it goes) and union hangs the smaller tree under the larger one's root. If union returns False, the two items were already connected: that's how cycles are detected.

Template A · DSU with path halving and union by size

The question it answersMerge groups and ask whether two items are in the same group, many times.
What it keepsparent[x] (x's boss), size[root], and the number of components.
When it checks for an answerunion compares the two roots; equal roots mean the items were already connected.
Use it whenNumber of provinces/components (LC 547, 323), redundant connection / cycle in an undirected graph (LC 684), Kruskal's MST, accounts merge (LC 721).
Not forSplitting groups apart (DSU can't undo unions); shortest paths.
Memory hook: "Ask for the boss's boss until you reach the CEO; merge companies by their CEOs"Each person reports to a boss; the CEO reports to themself. Two people are in the same company if they have the same CEO. To merge two companies, the smaller company's CEO starts reporting to the bigger company's CEO. While climbing to the CEO, people skip a level (report to their grand-boss), which keeps the chains short.

The story, mapped to the code. Each node is an employee; parent is their boss.

In the storyIn the codeWhat it means
Everyone is their own CEOparent = list(range(n))n separate companies.
Climb to the CEOfind(x)Follow parent until parent[x] == x.

The template. Two short methods; both optimisations together make each operation nearly O(1).

class DSU:
    def __init__(self, n):
        self.parent = list(range(n))
        self.size = [1] * n
        self.components = n

    def find(self, x):
        while self.parent[x] != x:
            self.parent[x] = self.parent[self.parent[x]]
            x = self.parent[x]
        return x

    def union(self, a, b):
        ra, rb = self.find(a), self.find(b)
        if ra == rb:
            return False
        if self.size[ra] < self.size[rb]:
            ra, rb = rb, ra
        self.parent[rb] = ra
        self.size[ra] += self.size[rb]
        self.components -= 1
        return True
class DSU {
  parent: number[]; size: number[]; components: number;
  constructor(n: number) {
    this.parent = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);
    this.size = new Array(n).fill(1);
    this.components = n;
  }

  find(x: number): number {
    while (this.parent[x] !== x) {
      this.parent[x] = this.parent[this.parent[x]];
      x = this.parent[x];
    }
    return x;
  }

  union(a: number, b: number): boolean {
    let ra = this.find(a), rb = this.find(b);
    if (ra === rb) return false;
    if (this.size[ra] < this.size[rb]) [ra, rb] = [rb, ra];
    this.parent[rb] = ra;
    this.size[ra] += this.size[rb];
    this.components--;
    return true;
  }
}
static class DSU {
    int[] parent, size;
    int components;

    DSU(int n) {
        parent = new int[n];
        size = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) { parent[i] = i; size[i] = 1; }
        components = n;
    }

    int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    boolean union(int a, int b) {
        int ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra == rb) return false;
        if (size[ra] < size[rb]) { int t = ra; ra = rb; rb = t; }
        parent[rb] = ra;
        size[ra] += size[rb];
        components--;
        return true;
    }
}

Line by line.

LineWhat it doesIn the storyWhy here, and what breaks if it moves

Watch it run. Step through 5 nodes and unions (0,1), (1,2), (3,4), (2,0). The last union finds equal roots: a cycle. The second player links the items without calling find.

Linking items directly never notices that 2 and 0 are already connected: the last union returns True, rewires node 2, and the component count drops to 1 instead of 2.

Dry run (generated from the same trace as the first player above):

Invariant. Every node's parent chain ends at its group's root; two nodes are connected iff they have the same root; components = number of roots.

Complexity. Almost O(1) per operation (inverse Ackermann α(n), effectively ≤ 4) with both optimisations; O(n) space.

Mistakes this template invites:

  • Comparing items instead of roots. Ask for both CEOs.
  • Linking non-roots. Only a root's parent changes in union.
  • Decrementing components on a no-op union. Only when ra != rb.

Climb to the CEO; merge companies by their CEOs.

Dynamic connectivity / cycle in undirected edges / Kruskal → DSU.

Same root ⇔ same group.
The line people get wrong

Three quick questions (answer before opening):

union(2, 0) after (0,1), (1,2)?

False: already connected (a cycle).

Components after the example?

2: {0,1,2}, {3,4}.

Kruskal in one line?

Sort edges by weight; add each edge whose union returns True.

6. How to remember it forever

Memory hook: "Ask the boss"Two people are in the same group if they have the same boss. Merging groups = one boss starts reporting to the other.
How this hook works: what “Ask the boss” means

What the slogan means, phrase by phrase

“Ask the boss”
Every element points to a parent. Following parents up leads to the group's boss (the root). find(x) is asking who your boss is.
“same boss → same group”
Two elements are connected exactly when find(a) == find(b).
“one boss starts reporting to the other”
Union links one root under the other root. Nobody else changes, and no group is relabelled.

Why this picture fits the pattern: Union-find problems keep merging groups and asking "are these two together?" Relabelling a whole group on every merge is slow. Pointing one boss at another is one line, and path compression keeps the chains short.

The story → the code

In the storyIn the code
Who do you report to?parent[x]
You are the bossparent[x] == x
Ask the bossfind(x)
Shortcut the chain while askingparent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
One boss reports to the otherparent[rb] = ra
Number of groupscomponents, minus 1 per real merge

Watch it on numbers

Six people (0–5), unions (0,1), (2,3), (1,3), (4,5), (0,2).

  1. (0,1): different bosses, so 1 now reports to 0. (2,3): 3 reports to 2. Groups: 4.
  2. (1,3): ask the bosses. 1's boss is 0, 3's boss is 2. Different, so 2 reports to 0. Groups: 3.
  3. (4,5): 5 reports to 4. Groups: 2.
  4. (0,2): both bosses are 0, the same boss. Already one group, so this edge would close a cycle. Nothing changes. Final: 2 groups.

The trap it saves you from

Linking the people instead of their bosses (parent[a] = b), which splits groups. Subtracting a group when the bosses were already the same is the other mistake.

It still works when…

Redundant Connection: the first edge whose ends already share a boss. Accounts Merge: emails are the people, and accounts that share one email merge. If edges get removed over time, run the timeline backwards so groups only merge.

Picture

A forest of small trees; every question walks up to a root, and walking flattens the path behind you.

Chant

"Find the roots; different roots, link them, one fewer group."

Safety rule

"Union-find only merges." If edges disappear, run time backwards.

Medium 947. Most Stones Removed with Same Row or Column Google Amazon ArrayHash Map

Problem: A stone can be removed if another stone shares its row or column. Return the most stones that can be removed.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: stones = [[0,0],[0,1],[1,0],[1,2],[2,1],[2,2]]
Output: 5
Explanation: One way to remove 5 stones is as follows: 1. Remove stone [2,2] because it shares the same row as [2,1]. 2. Remove stone [2,1] because it shares the same column as [0,1]. 3. Remove stone [1,2] because it shares the same row as [1,0]. 4. Remove stone [1,0] because it shares the same column as [0,0]. 5. Remove stone [0,1] because it shares the same row as [0,0]. Stone [0,0] cannot be removed since it does not share a row/column with another stone still on the plane.
Example 2
Input: stones = [[0,0],[0,2],[1,1],[2,0],[2,2]]
Output: 3
Explanation: One way to make 3 moves is as follows: 1. Remove stone [2,2] because it shares the same row as [2,0]. 2. Remove stone [2,0] because it shares the same column as [0,0]. 3. Remove stone [0,2] because it shares the same row as [0,0]. Stones [0,0] and [1,1] cannot be removed since they do not share a row/column with another stone still on the plane.

Constraints: 1 ≤ stones.length ≤ 1000 · 0 ≤ xi, yi ≤ 10⁴ · No two stones are at the same coordinate point.

Hint 1

Which stones can end up removed together? Think of connected groups.

Hint 2

How many stones must remain in each group?

From brute force to the pattern: Trying removal orders with DFS is exponential; components give the answer in near-linear time.

Spot it: Stones sharing a row or column form connected groups, and each group can be reduced to one stone. So the answer is stones − components. Union-find on rows and columns (column ids offset to keep them distinct) finds the components.

Why not another pattern? Simulating removals in some order can get stuck; counting components gives the optimum directly.

Approach:

  1. For each stone, union row with ~col (a distinct key for columns).
  2. Count distinct roots among the used keys.
  3. Return len(stones) − roots.
class Solution:
    def removeStones(self, stones: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        parent = {}

        def find(x):
            parent.setdefault(x, x)
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for r, c in stones:
            parent[find(r)] = find(~c)  # a stone links its row and its column (~c keeps columns separate)
        components = len({find(x) for x in parent})
        return len(stones) - components  # each group keeps exactly one stone
function removeStones(stones: number[][]): number {
    const parent = new Map<number, number>();

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        if (!parent.has(x)) {
            parent.set(x, x);
        }
        while (parent.get(x) !== x) {
            parent.set(x, parent.get(parent.get(x)!)!);
            x = parent.get(x)!;
        }
        return x;
    };

    for (const [r, c] of stones) {
        parent.set(find(r), find(~c));  // a stone links its row and its column (~c keeps columns separate)
    }
    const components = new Set([...parent.keys()].map(find)).size;
    return stones.length - components;  // each group keeps exactly one stone
}
class Solution {
    private final Map<Integer, Integer> parent = new HashMap<>();

    public int removeStones(int[][] stones) {
        for (int[] s : stones) {
            parent.put(find(s[0]), find(~s[1]));  // a stone links its row and its column (~c keeps columns separate)
        }
        Set<Integer> roots = new HashSet<>();
        for (int x : new ArrayList<>(parent.keySet())) {
            roots.add(find(x));
        }
        return stones.length - roots.size();  // each group keeps exactly one stone
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        parent.putIfAbsent(x, x);
        while (parent.get(x) != x) {
            parent.put(x, parent.get(parent.get(x)));
            x = parent.get(x);
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. ~c is −c − 1, which can never collide with a row index ≥ 0.
  2. Within a connected group, stones can be removed leaf-first (think of a spanning tree) until one remains.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • One stone → 0.
  • All in one row.
  • Stones connected only through a chain.

Complexity: O(n · α(n)) time, O(n) space.

Medium 721. Accounts Merge Google Amazon Microsoft StringHash Map

Problem: Accounts sharing any email belong to the same person. Merge them: name followed by sorted emails (any order of accounts).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: accounts = [["John","johnsmith@mail.com","john_newyork@mail.com"],["John","johnsmith@mail.com","john00@mail.com"],["Mary","mary@mail.com"],["John","johnnybravo@mail.com"]]
Output: [["John","john00@mail.com","john_newyork@mail.com","johnsmith@mail.com"],["Mary","mary@mail.com"],["John","johnnybravo@mail.com"]]
Explanation: The first and second John's are the same person as they have the common email "johnsmith@mail.com". The third John and Mary are different people as none of their email addresses are used by other accounts. We could return these lists in any order, for example the answer [['Mary', 'mary@mail.com'], ['John', 'johnnybravo@mail.com'], ['John', 'john00@mail.com', 'john_newyork@mail.com', 'johnsmith@mail.com']] would still be accepted.
Example 2
Input: accounts = [["Gabe","Gabe0@m.co","Gabe3@m.co","Gabe1@m.co"],["Kevin","Kevin3@m.co","Kevin5@m.co","Kevin0@m.co"],["Ethan","Ethan5@m.co","Ethan4@m.co","Ethan0@m.co"],["Hanzo","Hanzo3@m.co","Hanzo1@m.co","Hanzo0@m.co"],["Fern","Fern5@m.co","Fern1@m.co","Fern0@m.co"]]
Output: [["Ethan","Ethan0@m.co","Ethan4@m.co","Ethan5@m.co"],["Gabe","Gabe0@m.co","Gabe1@m.co","Gabe3@m.co"],["Hanzo","Hanzo0@m.co","Hanzo1@m.co","Hanzo3@m.co"],["Kevin","Kevin0@m.co","Kevin3@m.co","Kevin5@m.co"],["Fern","Fern0@m.co","Fern1@m.co","Fern5@m.co"]]

Constraints: 1 ≤ accounts.length ≤ 1000 · 2 ≤ accounts[i].length ≤ 10 · 1 ≤ accounts[i][j].length ≤ 30 · accounts[i][0] consists of English letters. · accounts[i][j] (for j > 0) is a valid email.

Hint 1

What should the nodes of the graph be?

Hint 2

Union all emails in one account; then group by root.

From brute force to the pattern: Pairwise account comparison is quadratic; union-find over emails is near-linear.

Spot it: Emails are nodes; an account links all of its emails. Connected components = people → union-find over emails.

Why not another pattern? Comparing every pair of accounts for shared emails is O(a² · e).

Approach:

  1. For each account, union each email with the account's first email; remember each email's name.
  2. Group emails by find(email).
  3. Output [name] + sorted(emails) per group.
from collections import defaultdict

class Solution:
    def accountsMerge(self, accounts: List[List[str]]) -> List[List[str]]:
        parent = {}
        name_of = {}

        def find(x):
            parent.setdefault(x, x)
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for name, first, *rest in accounts:
            name_of[first] = name
            find(first)
            for email in rest:
                name_of[email] = name
                parent[find(email)] = find(first)  # same account: same person
        groups = defaultdict(list)
        for email in parent:
            groups[find(email)].append(email)
        return [[name_of[root]] + sorted(emails) for root, emails in groups.items()]
function accountsMerge(accounts: string[][]): string[][] {
    const parent = new Map<string, string>();
    const nameOf = new Map<string, string>();

    const find = (x: string): string => {
        if (!parent.has(x)) {
            parent.set(x, x);
        }
        while (parent.get(x) !== x) {
            parent.set(x, parent.get(parent.get(x)!)!);
            x = parent.get(x)!;
        }
        return x;
    };

    for (const [name, first, ...rest] of accounts) {
        nameOf.set(first, name);
        find(first);
        for (const email of rest) {
            nameOf.set(email, name);
            parent.set(find(email), find(first));  // same account: same person
        }
    }
    const groups = new Map<string, string[]>();
    for (const email of [...parent.keys()]) {
        const root = find(email);
        if (!groups.has(root)) {
            groups.set(root, []);
        }
        groups.get(root)!.push(email);
    }
    return [...groups].map(([root, emails]) => [nameOf.get(root)!, ...emails.sort()]);
}
class Solution {
    private final Map<String, String> parent = new LinkedHashMap<>();  // keeps first-seen order

    public List<List<String>> accountsMerge(List<List<String>> accounts) {
        Map<String, String> nameOf = new HashMap<>();
        for (List<String> account : accounts) {
            String name = account.get(0), first = account.get(1);
            nameOf.put(first, name);
            find(first);
            for (String email : account.subList(2, account.size())) {
                nameOf.put(email, name);
                parent.put(find(email), find(first));  // same account: same person
            }
        }
        Map<String, List<String>> groups = new LinkedHashMap<>();
        for (String email : new ArrayList<>(parent.keySet())) {
            groups.computeIfAbsent(find(email), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(email);
        }
        List<List<String>> result = new ArrayList<>();
        for (Map.Entry<String, List<String>> e : groups.entrySet()) {
            List<String> emails = e.getValue();
            Collections.sort(emails);
            List<String> row = new ArrayList<>();
            row.add(nameOf.get(e.getKey()));
            row.addAll(emails);
            result.add(row);
        }
        return result;
    }

    private String find(String x) {
        parent.putIfAbsent(x, x);
        while (!parent.get(x).equals(x)) {
            parent.put(x, parent.get(parent.get(x)));
            x = parent.get(x);
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Linking every email to the account's first email connects the whole account.
  2. A shared email links two accounts' components automatically.
  3. Names are the same within a person, so any email's name works.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Same name, different people (no shared email).
  • An account with one email.
  • Chains of accounts linked through different emails.

Complexity: O(E log E) time (sorting dominates), O(E) space for E emails.

Hard 1970. Last Day Where You Can Still Cross Google MatrixArray

Problem: Each day one cell floods. Return the last day you can still walk from the top row to the bottom row on land.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: row = 2, col = 2, cells = [[1,1],[2,1],[1,2],[2,2]]
Output: 2
Explanation: The above image depicts how the matrix changes each day starting from day 0. The last day where it is possible to cross from top to bottom is on day 2.
Example 2
Input: row = 2, col = 2, cells = [[1,1],[1,2],[2,1],[2,2]]
Output: 1
Explanation: The above image depicts how the matrix changes each day starting from day 0. The last day where it is possible to cross from top to bottom is on day 1.

Constraints: 2 ≤ row, col ≤ 2 * 10⁴ · 4 ≤ row * col ≤ 2 * 10⁴ · cells.length == row * col · 1 ≤ ri ≤ row · 1 ≤ ci ≤ col · All the values of cells are unique.

Hint 1

Union-find can't remove connections. Can you reverse the process?

Hint 2

Add virtual top and bottom nodes so crossing becomes a connectivity check.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking every day with BFS is O((rc)²); binary search + BFS is O(rc log rc); reverse union-find is near-linear.

Spot it: Flooding only removes connections, which union-find can't undo. Run time backwards: start fully flooded and turn cells back into land from the last day. With virtual TOP and BOTTOM nodes, the first day they connect is the answer.

Why not another pattern? Binary search on the day with BFS per check is O(rc log rc) — also fine; reverse union-find is a single pass.

Approach:

  1. Nodes 0..r·c − 1, plus TOP = r·c, BOTTOM = r·c + 1.
  2. For day from the last down to 1: make cells[day − 1] land; union with land neighbours; top-row cells with TOP, bottom-row with BOTTOM.
  3. If find(TOP) == find(BOTTOM), return day − 1 (that cell was still land on day − 1).
class Solution:
    def latestDayToCross(self, row: int, col: int, cells: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        TOP, BOTTOM = row * col, row * col + 1
        parent = list(range(row * col + 2))
        land = [[False] * col for _ in range(row)]

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        def union(a, b):
            parent[find(a)] = find(b)

        for day in range(len(cells), 0, -1):  # undo the floods, latest first
            r, c = cells[day - 1][0] - 1, cells[day - 1][1] - 1
            land[r][c] = True
            node = r * col + c
            if r == 0:
                union(node, TOP)
            if r == row - 1:
                union(node, BOTTOM)
            for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                if 0 <= nr < row and 0 <= nc < col and land[nr][nc]:
                    union(node, nr * col + nc)
            if find(TOP) == find(BOTTOM):
                return day - 1  # on day - 1 this cell was still land, and a path existed
        return 0
function latestDayToCross(row: number, col: number, cells: number[][]): number {
    const TOP = row * col, BOTTOM = row * col + 1;
    const parent = Array.from({ length: row * col + 2 }, (_, i) => i);
    const land: boolean[][] = Array.from({ length: row }, () => new Array(col).fill(false));

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    const union = (a: number, b: number): void => {
        parent[find(a)] = find(b);
    };

    for (let day = cells.length; day > 0; day--) {  // undo the floods, latest first
        const r = cells[day - 1][0] - 1, c = cells[day - 1][1] - 1;
        land[r][c] = true;
        const node = r * col + c;
        if (r === 0) {
            union(node, TOP);
        }
        if (r === row - 1) {
            union(node, BOTTOM);
        }
        for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
            if (0 <= nr && nr < row && 0 <= nc && nc < col && land[nr][nc]) {
                union(node, nr * col + nc);
            }
        }
        if (find(TOP) === find(BOTTOM)) {
            return day - 1;  // on day - 1 this cell was still land, and a path existed
        }
    }
    return 0;
}
class Solution {
    private int[] parent;

    public int latestDayToCross(int row, int col, int[][] cells) {
        int TOP = row * col, BOTTOM = row * col + 1;
        parent = new int[row * col + 2];
        for (int i = 0; i < parent.length; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
        boolean[][] land = new boolean[row][col];
        int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        for (int day = cells.length; day > 0; day--) {  // undo the floods, latest first
            int r = cells[day - 1][0] - 1, c = cells[day - 1][1] - 1;
            land[r][c] = true;
            int node = r * col + c;
            if (r == 0) {
                union(node, TOP);
            }
            if (r == row - 1) {
                union(node, BOTTOM);
            }
            for (int[] d : dirs) {
                int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
                if (0 <= nr && nr < row && 0 <= nc && nc < col && land[nr][nc]) {
                    union(node, nr * col + nc);
                }
            }
            if (find(TOP) == find(BOTTOM)) {
                return day - 1;  // on day - 1 this cell was still land, and a path existed
            }
        }
        return 0;
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }

    private void union(int a, int b) {
        parent[find(a)] = find(b);
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Going backwards, land only appears, so connections only form: exactly what union-find supports.
  2. The virtual TOP and BOTTOM nodes turn "any top cell to any bottom cell" into one connectivity question.
  3. When restoring the cell flooded on day creates the connection, the land on day day − 1 has a crossing.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • One column.
  • A crossing only via a winding path.
  • The first flood already blocks everything.

Complexity: O(r · c · α(r · c)) time and space.

8. Common mistakes

Linking the nodes instead of their rootsparent[a] = b without find can split a set's tree and lose members. Always link find(a) to find(b).
Counting a union that didn't mergeDecrement the component count only when the roots differ.
Recursive find on deep treesWithout compression, a recursive find can hit Python's recursion limit. Use the iterative loop.
Mixing id spacesRows and columns, or cells and virtual nodes, need distinct ids (~col, rows * cols, …).
Trying to delete edgesUnion-find can't split sets; reverse the timeline (Last Day Where You Can Still Cross) or use another approach.

9. Self-check quiz

Edges arrive one at a time; after each, report the number of connected components. Best tool?

Each edge is one union in near-constant time; the component count updates in O(1).

union(a, b) finds the same root for a and b. What does that mean?

Equal roots mean the two were in one set already, so adding the edge creates a cycle.

Cells flood one per day; when can you no longer cross? How does union-find help?

Backwards in time, land only appears, so sets only merge.

What makes union-find operations nearly constant time?

Together they keep the trees extremely shallow: amortised O(α(n)).

Hard 305. Number of Islands II Google Amazon MatrixArray

Problem: An m × n grid starts as water. After each addLand position, return the number of islands.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ (Premium)

Example 1
Input: m = 3, n = 3, positions = [[0,0],[0,1],[1,2],[2,1]]
Output: [1,1,2,3]
Explanation: (0,1) joins the island at (0,0); (1,2) and (2,1) each start a new island.
Example 2
Input: m = 1, n = 1, positions = [[0,0]]
Output: [1]

Constraints: 1 ≤ m, n, positions.length ≤ 10⁴ · 1 ≤ m * n ≤ 10⁴ · positions[i].length == 2 · 0 ≤ ri < m · 0 ≤ ci < n

Hint 1

Islands only ever merge as land appears.

Hint 2

Use union-find: each new cell is a new island, and each merge with a different neighbouring island removes one.

From brute force to the pattern: Counting islands with BFS after every addition is O(k · mn); union-find is near O(k).

Spot it: Islands only merge as land is added, never split → union-find handles each addition in near-constant time: the new cell is a new island, and each union with a neighbouring island of a different root removes one.

Why not another pattern? Re-running a flood-fill count after every addition is O(k · m · n).

Approach:

  1. parent dict for land cells only; islands = 0.
  2. Add (r, c) (skip duplicates): parent[cell] = cell, islands += 1.
  3. For each land neighbour: if its root differs, union and islands −= 1.
  4. Record islands.
class Solution:
    def numIslands2(self, m: int, n: int, positions: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        parent = {}  # land cell -> parent cell

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]  # path halving
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        islands = 0
        result = []
        for r, c in positions:
            cell = (r, c)
            if cell not in parent:  # adding land twice changes nothing
                parent[cell] = cell
                islands += 1  # a brand-new island
                for nb in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1)):
                    if nb in parent:
                        a, b = find(cell), find(nb)
                        if a != b:
                            parent[a] = b  # two islands become one
                            islands -= 1
            result.append(islands)
        return result
function numIslands2(m: number, n: number, positions: number[][]): number[] {
    const parent = new Map<number, number>();  // land cell (r * n + c) -> parent cell

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent.get(x) !== x) {
            parent.set(x, parent.get(parent.get(x)!)!);  // path halving
            x = parent.get(x)!;
        }
        return x;
    };

    let islands = 0;
    const result: number[] = [];
    for (const [r, c] of positions) {
        const cell = r * n + c;
        if (!parent.has(cell)) {  // adding land twice changes nothing
            parent.set(cell, cell);
            islands += 1;  // a brand-new island
            for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
                const nb = nr * n + nc;
                if (0 <= nr && nr < m && 0 <= nc && nc < n && parent.has(nb)) {
                    const a = find(cell), b = find(nb);
                    if (a !== b) {
                        parent.set(a, b);  // two islands become one
                        islands -= 1;
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        result.push(islands);
    }
    return result;
}
class Solution {
    private final Map<Integer, Integer> parent = new HashMap<>();  // land cell (r * n + c) -> parent cell

    public List<Integer> numIslands2(int m, int n, int[][] positions) {
        int islands = 0;
        List<Integer> result = new ArrayList<>();
        int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        for (int[] p : positions) {
            int r = p[0], c = p[1];
            int cell = r * n + c;
            if (!parent.containsKey(cell)) {  // adding land twice changes nothing
                parent.put(cell, cell);
                islands += 1;  // a brand-new island
                for (int[] d : dirs) {
                    int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
                    int nb = nr * n + nc;
                    if (0 <= nr && nr < m && 0 <= nc && nc < n && parent.containsKey(nb)) {
                        int a = find(cell), b = find(nb);
                        if (a != b) {
                            parent.put(a, b);  // two islands become one
                            islands -= 1;
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
            result.add(islands);
        }
        return result;
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent.get(x) != x) {
            parent.put(x, parent.get(parent.get(x)));  // path halving
            x = parent.get(x);
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Only land cells are stored, so the grid is never allocated.
  2. Each successful union merges two different islands, reducing the count by one.
  3. A neighbour already in the same set (e.g. two neighbours of one island) doesn't change the count.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • The same position added twice.
  • A cell that joins three islands at once.
  • 1×1 grid.

Complexity: O(k · α(k)) time for k additions, O(k) space.

Hard 827. Making A Large Island Google Meta Amazon Microsoft MatrixHash Set

Problem: Change at most one 0 to 1. Return the size of the largest island possible.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: grid = [[1,0],[0,1]]
Output: 3
Explanation: Change one 0 to 1 and connect two 1s, then we get an island with area = 3.
Example 2
Input: grid = [[1,1],[1,0]]
Output: 4
Explanation: Change the 0 to 1 and make the island bigger, only one island with area = 4.

Constraints: n == grid.length · n == grid[i].length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 500 · grid[i][j] is either 0 or 1.

Hint 1

Measure every island once, before trying flips.

Hint 2

A flipped 0 connects the different islands adjacent to it; don't count the same island twice.

From brute force to the pattern: Flip + BFS for every zero is O(n⁴); precomputed sizes make each zero O(1).

Spot it: Precompute every island's component id and size (union-find or flood fill). Flipping a 0 joins the distinct islands next to it, so its result is 1 + Σ sizes of the distinct neighbouring ids.

Why not another pattern? Flipping each 0 and re-measuring with BFS is O(n⁴).

Approach:

  1. Union-find over land cells, tracking component sizes.
  2. For each 0: collect the roots of its land neighbours in a set; candidate 1 + Σ size[root].
  3. Answer: the max candidate, or n² if there's no 0.
class Solution:
    def largestIsland(self, grid: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(grid)
        parent = list(range(n * n))
        size = [1] * (n * n)

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for r in range(n):
            for c in range(n):
                if grid[r][c]:
                    for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r, c + 1)):
                        if nr < n and nc < n and grid[nr][nc]:
                            a, b = find(r * n + c), find(nr * n + nc)
                            if a != b:
                                parent[a] = b
                                size[b] += size[a]  # island sizes add up
        best = max((size[find(i)] for i in range(n * n) if grid[i // n][i % n]), default=0)
        for r in range(n):
            for c in range(n):
                if grid[r][c] == 0:
                    roots = {find(nr * n + nc) for nr, nc in ((r + 1, c), (r - 1, c), (r, c + 1), (r, c - 1))
                             if 0 <= nr < n and 0 <= nc < n and grid[nr][nc]}  # distinct neighbouring islands
                    best = max(best, 1 + sum(size[x] for x in roots))
        return best
function largestIsland(grid: number[][]): number {
    const n = grid.length;
    const parent = Array.from({ length: n * n }, (_, i) => i);
    const size: number[] = new Array(n * n).fill(1);

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    for (let r = 0; r < n; r++) {
        for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            if (grid[r][c]) {
                for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r, c + 1]]) {
                    if (nr < n && nc < n && grid[nr][nc]) {
                        const a = find(r * n + c), b = find(nr * n + nc);
                        if (a !== b) {
                            parent[a] = b;
                            size[b] += size[a];  // island sizes add up
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
    }
    let best = 0;
    for (let i = 0; i < n * n; i++) {
        if (grid[Math.floor(i / n)][i % n]) {
            best = Math.max(best, size[find(i)]);
        }
    }
    for (let r = 0; r < n; r++) {
        for (let c = 0; c < n; c++) {
            if (grid[r][c] === 0) {
                const roots = new Set<number>();  // distinct neighbouring islands
                for (const [nr, nc] of [[r + 1, c], [r - 1, c], [r, c + 1], [r, c - 1]]) {
                    if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n && grid[nr][nc]) {
                        roots.add(find(nr * n + nc));
                    }
                }
                let total = 1;
                for (const x of roots) {
                    total += size[x];
                }
                best = Math.max(best, total);
            }
        }
    }
    return best;
}
class Solution {
    private int[] parent;

    public int largestIsland(int[][] grid) {
        int n = grid.length;
        parent = new int[n * n];
        int[] size = new int[n * n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n * n; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
            size[i] = 1;
        }
        for (int r = 0; r < n; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                if (grid[r][c] == 1) {
                    for (int[] nb : new int[][] {{r + 1, c}, {r, c + 1}}) {
                        int nr = nb[0], nc = nb[1];
                        if (nr < n && nc < n && grid[nr][nc] == 1) {
                            int a = find(r * n + c), b = find(nr * n + nc);
                            if (a != b) {
                                parent[a] = b;
                                size[b] += size[a];  // island sizes add up
                            }
                        }
                    }
                }
            }
        }
        int best = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n * n; i++) {
            if (grid[i / n][i % n] == 1) {
                best = Math.max(best, size[find(i)]);
            }
        }
        int[][] dirs = {{1, 0}, {-1, 0}, {0, 1}, {0, -1}};
        for (int r = 0; r < n; r++) {
            for (int c = 0; c < n; c++) {
                if (grid[r][c] == 0) {
                    Set<Integer> roots = new HashSet<>();  // distinct neighbouring islands
                    for (int[] d : dirs) {
                        int nr = r + d[0], nc = c + d[1];
                        if (0 <= nr && nr < n && 0 <= nc && nc < n && grid[nr][nc] == 1) {
                            roots.add(find(nr * n + nc));
                        }
                    }
                    int total = 1;
                    for (int x : roots) {
                        total += size[x];
                    }
                    best = Math.max(best, total);
                }
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Cells are numbered r · n + c for the union-find arrays.
  2. The set removes duplicates when the same island touches the 0 from two sides.
  3. If the grid has no 0, the answer is the existing largest island (all ones → n²).

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • All ones → n².
  • All zeros → 1.
  • One island touching a zero on two sides.

Complexity: O(n² · α(n²)) time, O(n²) space.

Medium 1101. The Earliest Moment When Everyone Become Friends Google Array

Problem: Friendship is transitive. Given [timestamp, x, y] logs, return the earliest time everyone is acquainted, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗ (Premium)

Example 1
Input: logs = [[20190101,0,1],[20190104,3,4],[20190107,2,3],[20190211,1,5],[20190224,2,4],[20190301,0,3],[20190312,1,2],[20190322,4,5]], n = 6
Output: 20190301
Explanation: At 20190301 the groups {0,1,5} and {2,3,4} join, so everyone is connected.
Example 2
Input: logs = [[0,2,0],[1,0,1],[3,0,3],[4,1,2],[7,3,1]], n = 4
Output: 3

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 100 · 1 ≤ logs.length ≤ 10⁴ · logs[i].length == 3 · 0 ≤ timestampi ≤ 10⁹ · 0 ≤ xi, yi ≤ n - 1 · xi != yi · All the values timestampi are unique · All the pairs (xi, yi) occur at most one time in the input

Hint 1

Process events in time order.

Hint 2

Track how many friend groups exist with union-find.

From brute force to the pattern: Checking connectivity with BFS after every log is O(L · (n + L)); union-find is near-linear.

Spot it: Groups only merge over time → process logs in time order with union-find, counting groups. The first time the count reaches 1 is the answer.

Why not another pattern? Rebuilding the graph and checking connectivity after every log is O(logs · n).

Approach:

  1. Sort logs by timestamp; groups = n.
  2. For each log: if x and y have different roots, union and groups −= 1.
  3. When groups == 1, return the timestamp; otherwise −1.
class Solution:
    def earliestAcq(self, logs: List[List[int]], n: int) -> int:
        parent = list(range(n))

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        groups = n
        for t, x, y in sorted(logs):  # in time order
            a, b = find(x), find(y)
            if a != b:
                parent[a] = b
                groups -= 1  # two friend groups merge
                if groups == 1:
                    return t  # everyone is connected now
        return -1
function earliestAcq(logs: number[][], n: number): number {
    const parent = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    let groups = n;
    // in time order
    for (const [t, x, y] of [...logs].sort((p, q) => p[0] - q[0] || p[1] - q[1] || p[2] - q[2])) {
        const a = find(x), b = find(y);
        if (a !== b) {
            parent[a] = b;
            groups -= 1;  // two friend groups merge
            if (groups === 1) {
                return t;  // everyone is connected now
            }
        }
    }
    return -1;
}
class Solution {
    private int[] parent;

    public int earliestAcq(int[][] logs, int n) {
        parent = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
        int[][] sorted = logs.clone();
        // in time order
        Arrays.sort(sorted, (p, q) -> p[0] != q[0] ? Integer.compare(p[0], q[0])
                : p[1] != q[1] ? Integer.compare(p[1], q[1]) : Integer.compare(p[2], q[2]));
        int groups = n;
        for (int[] log : sorted) {
            int a = find(log[1]), b = find(log[2]);
            if (a != b) {
                parent[a] = b;
                groups -= 1;  // two friend groups merge
                if (groups == 1) {
                    return log[0];  // everyone is connected now
                }
            }
        }
        return -1;
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Each merge of two different groups reduces the number of groups by one.
  2. Logs between people already in the same group change nothing.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Never fully connected → −1.
  • Logs not sorted.
  • n = 1 (never happens per constraints, but 0 groups to merge).

Complexity: O(L log L + L · α(n)) time, O(n) space.

Medium 1722. Minimize Hamming Distance After Swap Operations Google ArrayHash Map

Problem: Swaps between given index pairs can be done any number of times. Minimise the Hamming distance between source and target.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: source = [1,2,3,4], target = [2,1,4,5], allowedSwaps = [[0,1],[2,3]]
Output: 1
Explanation: source can be transformed the following way: - Swap indices 0 and 1: source = [2,1,3,4] - Swap indices 2 and 3: source = [2,1,4,3] The Hamming distance of source and target is 1 as they differ in 1 position: index 3.
Example 2
Input: source = [1,2,3,4], target = [1,3,2,4], allowedSwaps = []
Output: 2
Explanation: There are no allowed swaps. The Hamming distance of source and target is 2 as they differ in 2 positions: index 1 and index 2.

Constraints: n == source.length == target.length · 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ source[i], target[i] ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ allowedSwaps.length ≤ 10⁵ · allowedSwaps[i].length == 2 · 0 ≤ ai, bi ≤ n - 1 · ai != bi

Hint 1

If you can swap (a, b) and (b, c), can you rearrange a, b, c in any order?

Hint 2

Group indices into components and compare value counts inside each.

From brute force to the pattern: Exploring swap sequences is exponential; components + counting is linear.

Spot it: Swaps compose: indices in the same union-find component can be permuted arbitrarily. So per component, the matches are the multiset overlap between source values and target values.

Why not another pattern? Simulating swaps or searching permutations is exponential.

Approach:

  1. Union the index pairs.
  2. Per component root: counter of source values.
  3. For each index, if its target value is available in its component's counter, use it; otherwise count a mismatch.
from collections import Counter, defaultdict

class Solution:
    def minimumHammingDistance(self, source: List[int], target: List[int], allowedSwaps: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        n = len(source)
        parent = list(range(n))

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for a, b in allowedSwaps:
            parent[find(a)] = find(b)  # these positions can exchange values
        available = defaultdict(Counter)  # component -> source values it holds
        for i, x in enumerate(source):
            available[find(i)][x] += 1
        distance = 0
        for i, t in enumerate(target):
            pool = available[find(i)]
            if pool[t]:
                pool[t] -= 1  # some source value in this component can be moved here
            else:
                distance += 1
        return distance
function minimumHammingDistance(source: number[], target: number[], allowedSwaps: number[][]): number {
    const n = source.length;
    const parent = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    for (const [a, b] of allowedSwaps) {
        parent[find(a)] = find(b);  // these positions can exchange values
    }
    const available = new Map<number, Map<number, number>>();  // component -> source values it holds
    source.forEach((x, i) => {
        const root = find(i);
        if (!available.has(root)) {
            available.set(root, new Map());
        }
        const pool = available.get(root)!;
        pool.set(x, (pool.get(x) ?? 0) + 1);
    });
    let distance = 0;
    target.forEach((t, i) => {
        const pool = available.get(find(i)) ?? new Map<number, number>();
        if (pool.get(t)) {
            pool.set(t, pool.get(t)! - 1);  // some source value in this component can be moved here
        } else {
            distance += 1;
        }
    });
    return distance;
}
class Solution {
    private int[] parent;

    public int minimumHammingDistance(int[] source, int[] target, int[][] allowedSwaps) {
        int n = source.length;
        parent = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
        for (int[] s : allowedSwaps) {
            parent[find(s[0])] = find(s[1]);  // these positions can exchange values
        }
        Map<Integer, Map<Integer, Integer>> available = new HashMap<>();  // component -> source values it holds
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            available.computeIfAbsent(find(i), k -> new HashMap<>()).merge(source[i], 1, Integer::sum);
        }
        int distance = 0;
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            Map<Integer, Integer> pool = available.getOrDefault(find(i), new HashMap<>());
            if (pool.getOrDefault(target[i], 0) > 0) {
                pool.merge(target[i], -1, Integer::sum);  // some source value in this component can be moved here
            } else {
                distance += 1;
            }
        }
        return distance;
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Adjacent transpositions within a connected set generate every permutation of that set.
  2. Matching target values against the component's multiset counts the best overlap.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • No swaps (plain Hamming distance).
  • Duplicate values.
  • Everything connected.

Complexity: O(n + s · α(n)) time, O(n) space.

Medium 2492. Minimum Score of a Path Between Two Cities Google Graph

Problem: A path's score is its smallest road. Paths may repeat roads and cities. Return the minimum score of a path from 1 to n.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 4, roads = [[1,2,9],[2,3,6],[2,4,5],[1,4,7]]
Output: 5
Explanation: The path from city 1 to 4 with the minimum score is: 1 -> 2 -> 4. The score of this path is min(9,5) = 5. It can be shown that no other path has less score.
Example 2
Input: n = 4, roads = [[1,2,2],[1,3,4],[3,4,7]]
Output: 2
Explanation: The path from city 1 to 4 with the minimum score is: 1 -> 2 -> 1 -> 3 -> 4. The score of this path is min(2,2,4,7) = 2.

Constraints: 2 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ roads.length ≤ 10⁵ · roads[i].length == 3 · 1 ≤ ai, bi ≤ n · ai != bi · 1 ≤ distancei ≤ 10⁴ · There are no repeated edges. · There is at least one path between 1 and n.

Hint 1

Paths can reuse roads. Which roads can a path from 1 to n include?

Hint 2

Find city 1's connected component.

From brute force to the pattern: Searching paths with a max-min objective is overkill; the component's smallest road is the answer.

Spot it: Because paths can wander and come back, any road in the same connected component as city 1 (and n) can be included. Find the component with union-find and take its smallest road.

Why not another pattern? Dijkstra-style path optimisation is unnecessary: the repetition rule removes the path structure.

Approach:

  1. Union all roads.
  2. Return the minimum distance among roads whose endpoints share city 1's root.
class Solution:
    def minScore(self, n: int, roads: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        parent = list(range(n + 1))

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for a, b, _ in roads:
            parent[find(a)] = find(b)
        root = find(1)
        return min(d for a, b, d in roads if find(a) == root)  # any road reachable from city 1
function minScore(n: number, roads: number[][]): number {
    const parent = Array.from({ length: n + 1 }, (_, i) => i);

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    for (const [a, b] of roads) {
        parent[find(a)] = find(b);
    }
    const root = find(1);
    return Math.min(...roads.filter(([a]) => find(a) === root).map((r) => r[2]));  // any road reachable from city 1
}
class Solution {
    private int[] parent;

    public int minScore(int n, int[][] roads) {
        parent = new int[n + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i <= n; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
        for (int[] r : roads) {
            parent[find(r[0])] = find(r[1]);
        }
        int root = find(1);
        int best = Integer.MAX_VALUE;
        for (int[] r : roads) {
            if (find(r[0]) == root) {
                best = Math.min(best, r[2]);  // any road reachable from city 1
            }
        }
        return best;
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. From city 1 you can detour to any road in its component and come back, then continue to n.
  2. Both endpoints of a road are in the same component, so checking one is enough.
