  • Disconnected parts with smaller roads (ignored).
  • A single road.
  • The smallest road on a dead-end branch.

Complexity: O(E · α(n)) time, O(n) space.

Medium 3532. Path Existence Queries in a Graph I Google Amazon Microsoft Array

Problem: Nodes i, j are linked if |nums[i] − nums[j]| ≤ maxDiff (nums sorted). Answer reachability queries.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 2, nums = [1,3], maxDiff = 1, queries = [[0,0],[0,1]]
Output: [true,false]
Explanation: Query [0,0]: Node 0 has a trivial path to itself. Query [0,1]: There is no edge between Node 0 and Node 1 because |nums[0] - nums[1]| = |1 - 3| = 2, which is greater than maxDiff. Thus, the final answer after processing all the queries is [true, false].
Example 2
Input: n = 4, nums = [2,5,6,8], maxDiff = 2, queries = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,3],[2,3]]
Output: [false,false,true,true]
Explanation: The resulting graph is: Query [0,1]: There is no edge between Node 0 and Node 1 because |nums[0] - nums[1]| = |2 - 5| = 3, which is greater than maxDiff. Query [0,2]: There is no edge between Node 0 and Node 2 because |nums[0] - nums[2]| = |2 - 6| = 4, which is greater than maxDiff. Query [1,3]: There is a path between Node 1 and Node 3 through Node 2 since |nums[1] - nums[2]| = |5 - 6| = 1 and |nums[2] - nums[3]| = |6 - 8| = 2, both of which are within maxDiff. Query [2,3]: There is an edge between Node 2 and Node 3 because |nums[2] - nums[3]| = |6 - 8| = 2, which is equal to maxDiff. Thus, the final answer after processing all the queries is [false, false, true, true].

Constraints: 1 ≤ n == nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁵ · nums is sorted in non-decreasing order. · 0 ≤ maxDiff ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ queries.length ≤ 10⁵ · queries[i] == [ui, vi] · 0 ≤ ui, vi < n

Hint 1

The array is sorted. When can two nodes on opposite sides of a big gap be connected?

Hint 2

Components are contiguous segments.

From brute force to the pattern: All pairwise edges + BFS is O(n²); scanning gaps is O(n).

Spot it: With sorted values, if i reaches some j > i + 1, then each step in between also has a small gap, so components are contiguous runs broken where nums[i+1] − nums[i] > maxDiff. Label runs (a 1D union-find).

Why not another pattern? Building all O(n²) edges is too slow.

Approach:

  1. group[0] = 0; group[i] = group[i − 1] + (gap > maxDiff).
  2. Query: group[u] == group[v].
class Solution:
    def pathExistenceQueries(self, n: int, nums: List[int], maxDiff: int, queries: List[List[int]]) -> List[bool]:
        group = [0] * n
        for i in range(1, n):
            group[i] = group[i - 1] + (nums[i] - nums[i - 1] > maxDiff)  # a big gap starts a new component
        return [group[u] == group[v] for u, v in queries]
function pathExistenceQueries(n: number, nums: number[], maxDiff: number, queries: number[][]): boolean[] {
    const group: number[] = new Array(n).fill(0);
    for (let i = 1; i < n; i++) {
        group[i] = group[i - 1] + (nums[i] - nums[i - 1] > maxDiff ? 1 : 0);  // a big gap starts a new component
    }
    return queries.map(([u, v]) => group[u] === group[v]);
}
class Solution {
    public boolean[] pathExistenceQueries(int n, int[] nums, int maxDiff, int[][] queries) {
        int[] group = new int[n];
        for (int i = 1; i < n; i++) {
            group[i] = group[i - 1] + (nums[i] - nums[i - 1] > maxDiff ? 1 : 0);  // a big gap starts a new component
        }
        boolean[] answer = new boolean[queries.length];
        for (int q = 0; q < queries.length; q++) {
            answer[q] = group[queries[q][0]] == group[queries[q][1]];
        }
        return answer;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. If adjacent sorted values are close, they're directly linked, so a run of close neighbours is connected.
  2. A gap larger than maxDiff can't be jumped by anyone, since every pair across it differs even more.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • u == v.
  • Equal values.
  • Every gap too large.

Complexity: O(n + q) time, O(n) space.

Hard 3534. Path Existence Queries in a Graph II Google Array

Problem: Same graph but nums is unsorted, and queries ask for the shortest path length (−1 if unreachable).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 5, nums = [1,8,3,4,2], maxDiff = 3, queries = [[0,3],[2,4]]
Output: [1,1]
Explanation: The resulting graph is: Query Shortest Path Minimum Distance [0, 3] 0 → 3 1 [2, 4] 2 → 4 1 Thus, the output is [1, 1].
Example 2
Input: n = 5, nums = [5,3,1,9,10], maxDiff = 2, queries = [[0,1],[0,2],[2,3],[4,3]]
Output: [1,2,-1,1]
Explanation: The resulting graph is:

Constraints: 1 ≤ n == nums.length ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ nums[i] ≤ 10⁵ · 0 ≤ maxDiff ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ queries.length ≤ 10⁵ · queries[i] == [ui, vi] · 0 ≤ ui, vi < n

Hint 1

Sort the values. From a node, which reachable node is the best next step?

Hint 2

Greedy farthest jumps give shortest paths; count jumps quickly with binary lifting.

From brute force to the pattern: BFS per query is O(q · n²) on the implicit graph; greedy jumps with binary lifting are O(log n) per query.

Spot it: In sorted order, the best move from a node is to the farthest position still within maxDiff (greedy jumps, like Jump Game II). Precompute that with two pointers, then binary lifting answers each query in O(log n).

Why not another pattern? BFS per query is O(n²) per query.

Approach:

  1. Sort indices by value; pos[node] = its sorted position.
  2. reach[p] = largest q with vals[q] − vals[p] ≤ maxDiff (two pointers); up[0] = reach, up[j] = up[j−1] ∘ up[j−1].
  3. Query a < b (positions): jump with the largest powers while up[j][a] < b, counting 2^j; then one more jump if reach[a] ≥ b, else −1.
class Solution:
    def pathExistenceQueries(self, n: int, nums: List[int], maxDiff: int, queries: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        order = sorted(range(n), key=lambda i: nums[i])
        pos = [0] * n
        for p, i in enumerate(order):
            pos[i] = p
        vals = [nums[i] for i in order]
        reach = [0] * n  # farthest sorted position reachable in one step
        q = 0
        for p in range(n):
            q = max(q, p)
            while q + 1 < n and vals[q + 1] - vals[p] <= maxDiff:
                q += 1
            reach[p] = q
        up = [reach]  # up[j][p]: position after 2^j greedy jumps
        for _ in range(n.bit_length()):
            prev = up[-1]
            up.append([prev[prev[p]] for p in range(n)])
        answer = []
        for u, v in queries:
            a, b = sorted((pos[u], pos[v]))
            if a == b:
                answer.append(0)
                continue
            jumps = 0
            for j in range(len(up) - 1, -1, -1):
                if up[j][a] < b:
                    a = up[j][a]  # still short of b: take these 2^j jumps
                    jumps += 1 << j
            answer.append(jumps + 1 if reach[a] >= b else -1)  # one more jump, or stuck
        return answer
function pathExistenceQueries(n: number, nums: number[], maxDiff: number, queries: number[][]): number[] {
    const order = nums.map((_, i) => i).sort((a, b) => nums[a] - nums[b] || a - b);
    const pos: number[] = new Array(n).fill(0);
    order.forEach((i, p) => {
        pos[i] = p;
    });
    const vals = order.map((i) => nums[i]);
    const reach: number[] = new Array(n).fill(0);  // farthest sorted position reachable in one step
    let q = 0;
    for (let p = 0; p < n; p++) {
        q = Math.max(q, p);
        while (q + 1 < n && vals[q + 1] - vals[p] <= maxDiff) {
            q += 1;
        }
        reach[p] = q;
    }
    const up: number[][] = [reach];  // up[j][p]: position after 2^j greedy jumps
    const bitLength = 32 - Math.clz32(n);
    for (let t = 0; t < bitLength; t++) {
        const prev = up[up.length - 1];
        up.push(prev.map((x) => prev[x]));
    }
    const answer: number[] = [];
    for (const [u, v] of queries) {
        let a = Math.min(pos[u], pos[v]);
        const b = Math.max(pos[u], pos[v]);
        if (a === b) {
            answer.push(0);
            continue;
        }
        let jumps = 0;
        for (let j = up.length - 1; j >= 0; j--) {
            if (up[j][a] < b) {
                a = up[j][a];  // still short of b: take these 2^j jumps
                jumps += 2 ** j;
            }
        }
        answer.push(reach[a] >= b ? jumps + 1 : -1);  // one more jump, or stuck
    }
    return answer;
}
class Solution {
    public int[] pathExistenceQueries(int n, int[] nums, int maxDiff, int[][] queries) {
        Integer[] order = new Integer[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            order[i] = i;
        }
        Arrays.sort(order, (a, b) -> nums[a] != nums[b] ? Integer.compare(nums[a], nums[b]) : Integer.compare(a, b));
        int[] pos = new int[n];
        int[] vals = new int[n];
        for (int p = 0; p < n; p++) {
            pos[order[p]] = p;
            vals[p] = nums[order[p]];
        }
        int[] reach = new int[n];  // farthest sorted position reachable in one step
        int q = 0;
        for (int p = 0; p < n; p++) {
            q = Math.max(q, p);
            while (q + 1 < n && vals[q + 1] - vals[p] <= maxDiff) {
                q += 1;
            }
            reach[p] = q;
        }
        List<int[]> up = new ArrayList<>();  // up.get(j)[p]: position after 2^j greedy jumps
        up.add(reach);
        int bitLength = 32 - Integer.numberOfLeadingZeros(n);
        for (int t = 0; t < bitLength; t++) {
            int[] prev = up.get(up.size() - 1);
            int[] next = new int[n];
            for (int p = 0; p < n; p++) {
                next[p] = prev[prev[p]];
            }
            up.add(next);
        }
        int[] answer = new int[queries.length];
        for (int k = 0; k < queries.length; k++) {
            int a = Math.min(pos[queries[k][0]], pos[queries[k][1]]);
            int b = Math.max(pos[queries[k][0]], pos[queries[k][1]]);
            if (a == b) {
                answer[k] = 0;
                continue;
            }
            int jumps = 0;
            for (int j = up.size() - 1; j >= 0; j--) {
                if (up.get(j)[a] < b) {
                    a = up.get(j)[a];  // still short of b: take these 2^j jumps
                    jumps += 1 << j;
                }
            }
            answer[k] = reach[a] >= b ? jumps + 1 : -1;  // one more jump, or stuck
        }
        return answer;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Jumping to the farthest reachable position is never worse: anything reachable from a nearer position is reachable from the farther one too.
  2. Binary lifting takes jumps in powers of two while staying short of the target, then checks the final jump.
  3. If the greedy walk gets stuck (reach[a] == a), the target is in another component: −1.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Same node → 0.
  • Different components → −1.
  • Equal values.

Complexity: O((n + q) log n) time, O(n log n) space.

Medium 684. Redundant Connection Start here Amazon Microsoft Graph

Problem: A tree had one extra edge added. Return the edge to remove (the last such edge in the input if several work).

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: edges = [[1,2],[1,3],[2,3]]
Output: [2,3]
Example 2
Input: edges = [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[1,4],[1,5]]
Output: [1,4]

Constraints: n == edges.length · 3 ≤ n ≤ 1000 · edges[i].length == 2 · 1 ≤ ai < bi ≤ edges.length · ai != bi · There are no repeated edges. · The given graph is connected.

Hint 1

Add edges one by one. When does an edge become redundant?

Hint 2

Use union-find to check if its endpoints are already connected.

From brute force to the pattern: Removing each edge and testing is O(n²); union-find is near-linear.

Spot it: Adding edges one by one, the extra edge is the one that joins two nodes already connected → union-find detects it immediately.

Why not another pattern? Removing each edge and checking connectivity is O(n²).

Approach:

  1. For each edge in order: if find(a) == find(b), return it.
  2. Otherwise union them.
class Solution:
    def findRedundantConnection(self, edges: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        parent = list(range(len(edges) + 1))

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for a, b in edges:
            ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
            if ra == rb:
                return [a, b]  # already connected: this edge closes the cycle
            parent[ra] = rb
        return []
function findRedundantConnection(edges: number[][]): number[] {
    const parent = Array.from({ length: edges.length + 1 }, (_, i) => i);

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    for (const [a, b] of edges) {
        const ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra === rb) {
            return [a, b];  // already connected: this edge closes the cycle
        }
        parent[ra] = rb;
    }
    return [];
}
class Solution {
    private int[] parent;

    public int[] findRedundantConnection(int[][] edges) {
        parent = new int[edges.length + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i < parent.length; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
        for (int[] e : edges) {
            int ra = find(e[0]), rb = find(e[1]);
            if (ra == rb) {
                return e;  // already connected: this edge closes the cycle
            }
            parent[ra] = rb;
        }
        return new int[0];
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. The graph has exactly one cycle; the first edge that closes it, in input order, is the last cycle edge to appear — the one the problem asks for.
  2. Every other edge joins two different components.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • The cycle includes the first edges.
  • Small cycle of length 3.
  • The extra edge is last.

Complexity: O(n · α(n)) time, O(n) space.

Medium 990. Satisfiability of Equality Equations Start here Amazon StringArray

Problem: Equations are a==b or a!=b over letters. Can all hold at once?

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: equations = ["a==b","b!=a"]
Output: false
Explanation: If we assign say, a = 1 and b = 1, then the first equation is satisfied, but not the second. There is no way to assign the variables to satisfy both equations.
Example 2
Input: equations = ["b==a","a==b"]
Output: true
Explanation: We could assign a = 1 and b = 1 to satisfy both equations.

Constraints: 1 ≤ equations.length ≤ 500 · equations[i].length == 4 · equations[i][0] is a lowercase letter. · equations[i][1] is either '=' or '!'. · equations[i][2] is '='. · equations[i][3] is a lowercase letter.

Hint 1

Which letters must end up equal?

Hint 2

Group them with union-find, then check the inequalities.

From brute force to the pattern: Assigning values is exponential; union-find is linear.

Spot it: Equalities are transitive → union-find groups letters that must be equal. Then each != must connect different groups.

Why not another pattern? Trying value assignments is exponential in the number of letters.

Approach:

  1. Union the two letters of every ==.
  2. For every !=, if both letters have the same root, return false.
class Solution:
    def equationsPossible(self, equations: List[str]) -> bool:
        parent = list(range(26))

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for e in equations:
            if e[1] == "=":
                parent[find(ord(e[0]) - 97)] = find(ord(e[3]) - 97)  # must be equal
        for e in equations:
            if e[1] == "!" and find(ord(e[0]) - 97) == find(ord(e[3]) - 97):
                return False  # forced equal, but required different
        return True
function equationsPossible(equations: string[]): boolean {
    const parent = Array.from({ length: 26 }, (_, i) => i);

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    const letter = (ch: string): number => ch.charCodeAt(0) - 97;
    for (const e of equations) {
        if (e[1] === "=") {
            parent[find(letter(e[0]))] = find(letter(e[3]));  // must be equal
        }
    }
    for (const e of equations) {
        if (e[1] === "!" && find(letter(e[0])) === find(letter(e[3]))) {
            return false;  // forced equal, but required different
        }
    }
    return true;
}
class Solution {
    private final int[] parent = new int[26];

    public boolean equationsPossible(String[] equations) {
        for (int i = 0; i < 26; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
        for (String e : equations) {
            if (e.charAt(1) == '=') {
                parent[find(e.charAt(0) - 'a')] = find(e.charAt(3) - 'a');  // must be equal
            }
        }
        for (String e : equations) {
            if (e.charAt(1) == '!' && find(e.charAt(0) - 'a') == find(e.charAt(3) - 'a')) {
                return false;  // forced equal, but required different
            }
        }
        return true;
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. All equalities must be applied before checking inequalities, because equality chains can come in any order.
  2. a != a is caught because a letter is always in its own group.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • a!=a → false.
  • Long equality chains.
  • Only inequalities → true.

Complexity: O(m · α(26)) time, O(1) space.

Medium 1319. Number of Operations to Make Network Connected Start here Amazon Graph

Problem: Move cables (each connects two computers) so all n computers are connected. Return the fewest moves, or −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: n = 4, connections = [[0,1],[0,2],[1,2]]
Output: 1
Explanation: Remove cable between computer 1 and 2 and place between computers 1 and 3.
Example 2
Input: n = 6, connections = [[0,1],[0,2],[0,3],[1,2],[1,3]]
Output: 2

Constraints: 1 ≤ n ≤ 10⁵ · 1 ≤ connections.length ≤ min(n * (n - 1) / 2, 10⁵) · connections[i].length == 2 · 0 ≤ ai, bi < n · ai != bi · There are no repeated connections. · No two computers are connected by more than one cable.

Hint 1

How many cables does a connected network need at minimum?

Hint 2

Count the components with union-find.

From brute force to the pattern: Simulating moves is complicated; counting components is near-linear.

Spot it: Each move can join two components, using a redundant cable. With at least n − 1 cables there are always enough spares, so the answer is components − 1, counted with union-find.

Why not another pattern? Simulating cable moves is unnecessary once the counting argument is clear.

Approach:

  1. If len(connections) < n − 1, return −1.
  2. Union all cables, counting successful unions.
  3. Return components − 1.
class Solution:
    def makeConnected(self, n: int, connections: List[List[int]]) -> int:
        if len(connections) < n - 1:
            return -1  # not enough cables to connect n computers
        parent = list(range(n))

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        components = n
        for a, b in connections:
            ra, rb = find(a), find(b)
            if ra != rb:
                parent[ra] = rb
                components -= 1
        return components - 1  # one move per extra component
function makeConnected(n: number, connections: number[][]): number {
    if (connections.length < n - 1) {
        return -1;  // not enough cables to connect n computers
    }
    const parent = Array.from({ length: n }, (_, i) => i);

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    let components = n;
    for (const [a, b] of connections) {
        const ra = find(a), rb = find(b);
        if (ra !== rb) {
            parent[ra] = rb;
            components -= 1;
        }
    }
    return components - 1;  // one move per extra component
}
class Solution {
    private int[] parent;

    public int makeConnected(int n, int[][] connections) {
        if (connections.length < n - 1) {
            return -1;  // not enough cables to connect n computers
        }
        parent = new int[n];
        for (int i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
        int components = n;
        for (int[] c : connections) {
            int ra = find(c[0]), rb = find(c[1]);
            if (ra != rb) {
                parent[ra] = rb;
                components -= 1;
            }
        }
        return components - 1;  // one move per extra component
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. A connected graph on n nodes needs n − 1 edges, so fewer cables can never work.
  2. Otherwise the redundant cables (those inside a component) are enough to link the components.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • Too few cables → −1.
  • Already connected → 0.
  • Isolated computers.

Complexity: O(m · α(n)) time, O(n) space.

Medium 3607. Power Grid Maintenance Cisco GraphHeapHash Set

Problem: Stations go offline over time (grids stay connected). For a check at x: x if online, else the smallest online id in its grid, else −1.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: c = 5, connections = [[1,2],[2,3],[3,4],[4,5]], queries = [[1,3],[2,1],[1,1],[2,2],[1,2]]
Output: [3,2,3]
Explanation: Initially, all stations {1, 2, 3, 4, 5} are online and form a single power grid. Query [1,3]: Station 3 is online, so the maintenance check is resolved by station 3. Query [2,1]: Station 1 goes offline. The remaining online stations are {2, 3, 4, 5}. Query [1,1]: Station 1 is offline, so the check is resolved by the operational station with the smallest id among {2, 3, 4, 5}, which is station 2. Query [2,2]: Station 2 goes offline. The remaining online stations are {3, 4, 5}. Query [1,2]: Station 2 is offline, so the check is resolved by the operational station with the smallest id among {3, 4, 5}, which is station 3.
Example 2
Input: c = 3, connections = [], queries = [[1,1],[2,1],[1,1]]
Output: [1,-1]
Explanation: There are no connections, so each station is its own isolated grid. Query [1,1]: Station 1 is online in its isolated grid, so the maintenance check is resolved by station 1. Query [2,1]: Station 1 goes offline. Query [1,1]: Station 1 is offline and there are no other stations in its grid, so the result is -1.
Hint 1

Does going offline change which stations are in the same grid?

Hint 2

For each grid, you need the smallest online id under deletions: a heap with lazy deletion.

From brute force to the pattern: Scanning a grid per query is O(c); lazy heaps are O(log c) amortised.

Spot it: Grids are fixed connected components → union-find once. Each component keeps a min-heap of its ids; offline stations are removed lazily when they reach the top.

Why not another pattern? Scanning a grid for its smallest online station per query is O(c) each.

Approach:

  1. Union all cables; heap of ids per root.
  2. Type 2: mark offline.
  3. Type 1: if online, answer x; else pop offline ids from its grid's heap and answer the top or −1.
import heapq

class Solution:
    def processQueries(self, c: int, connections: List[List[int]], queries: List[List[int]]) -> List[int]:
        parent = list(range(c + 1))

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for a, b in connections:
            parent[find(a)] = find(b)
        grid = {}  # root -> min-heap of station ids in that grid
        for s in range(1, c + 1):
            grid.setdefault(find(s), []).append(s)  # added in increasing order: already a heap
        offline = set()
        answer = []
        for kind, x in queries:
            if kind == 2:
                offline.add(x)
                continue
            if x not in offline:
                answer.append(x)  # it handles its own check
                continue
            heap = grid[find(x)]
            while heap and heap[0] in offline:
                heapq.heappop(heap)  # lazily drop stations that went offline
            answer.append(heap[0] if heap else -1)
        return answer
function processQueries(c: number, connections: number[][], queries: number[][]): number[] {
    const parent = Array.from({ length: c + 1 }, (_, i) => i);

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    for (const [a, b] of connections) {
        parent[find(a)] = find(b);
    }
    // root -> station ids in that grid, increasing; head[root] skips the ones already dropped
    const grid = new Map<number, number[]>();
    const head = new Map<number, number>();
    for (let s = 1; s <= c; s++) {
        const root = find(s);
        if (!grid.has(root)) {
            grid.set(root, []);
            head.set(root, 0);
        }
        grid.get(root)!.push(s);  // added in increasing order: the smallest is always in front
    }
    const offline = new Set<number>();
    const answer: number[] = [];
    for (const [kind, x] of queries) {
        if (kind === 2) {
            offline.add(x);
            continue;
        }
        if (!offline.has(x)) {
            answer.push(x);  // it handles its own check
            continue;
        }
        const root = find(x);
        const ids = grid.get(root)!;
        let h = head.get(root)!;
        while (h < ids.length && offline.has(ids[h])) {
            h += 1;  // lazily drop stations that went offline
        }
        head.set(root, h);
        answer.push(h < ids.length ? ids[h] : -1);
    }
    return answer;
}
class Solution {
    private int[] parent;

    public int[] processQueries(int c, int[][] connections, int[][] queries) {
        parent = new int[c + 1];
        for (int i = 0; i <= c; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
        for (int[] e : connections) {
            parent[find(e[0])] = find(e[1]);
        }
        Map<Integer, Deque<Integer>> grid = new HashMap<>();  // root -> station ids in that grid, smallest first
        for (int s = 1; s <= c; s++) {
            grid.computeIfAbsent(find(s), k -> new ArrayDeque<>()).offer(s);  // added in increasing order
        }
        Set<Integer> offline = new HashSet<>();
        List<Integer> answer = new ArrayList<>();
        for (int[] q : queries) {
            int kind = q[0], x = q[1];
            if (kind == 2) {
                offline.add(x);
                continue;
            }
            if (!offline.contains(x)) {
                answer.add(x);  // it handles its own check
                continue;
            }
            Deque<Integer> ids = grid.get(find(x));
            while (!ids.isEmpty() && offline.contains(ids.peek())) {
                ids.poll();  // lazily drop stations that went offline
            }
            answer.add(ids.isEmpty() ? -1 : ids.peek());
        }
        return answer.stream().mapToInt(Integer::intValue).toArray();
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Taking a station offline doesn't change connectivity, so the components are computed once.
  2. Stations never come back online, so a popped offline id never needs to return.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • All stations offline → −1.
  • Isolated stations.
  • Checking an online station.

Complexity: O((c + n) α(c) + q log c) time, O(c) space.

Medium 1202. Smallest String With Swaps Microsoft StringArray

Problem: Swap characters at any given pairs any number of times. Return the lexicographically smallest string.

Solve it on LeetCode ↗

Example 1
Input: s = "dcab", pairs = [[0,3],[1,2]]
Output: "bacd"
Explanation: Swap s[0] and s[3], s = "bcad" Swap s[1] and s[2], s = "bacd"
Example 2
Input: s = "dcab", pairs = [[0,3],[1,2],[0,2]]
Output: "abcd"
Explanation: Swap s[0] and s[3], s = "bcad" Swap s[0] and s[2], s = "acbd" Swap s[1] and s[2], s = "abcd"

Constraints: 1 ≤ s.length ≤ 10^5 · 0 ≤ pairs.length ≤ 10^5 · 0 ≤ pairs[i][0], pairs[i][1] < s.length · s only contains lower case English letters.

Hint 1

Which positions can exchange letters (even indirectly)?

Hint 2

Within such a group, which arrangement is smallest?

From brute force to the pattern: Searching swap sequences is exponential; components + sorting is near-linear.

Spot it: Swaps compose: indices in the same union-find component can be permuted freely, so give each component its characters in sorted order.

Why not another pattern? Simulating swaps can't reach every permutation efficiently.

Approach:

  1. Union all pairs.
  2. Group indices by root.
  3. Sort each group's characters and write them into its sorted indices.
from collections import defaultdict

class Solution:
    def smallestStringWithSwaps(self, s: str, pairs: List[List[int]]) -> str:
        parent = list(range(len(s)))

        def find(x):
            while parent[x] != x:
                parent[x] = parent[parent[x]]
                x = parent[x]
            return x

        for a, b in pairs:
            parent[find(a)] = find(b)
        groups = defaultdict(list)
        for i in range(len(s)):
            groups[find(i)].append(i)  # indices in increasing order
        out = list(s)
        for idx in groups.values():
            for i, ch in zip(idx, sorted(s[i] for i in idx)):
                out[i] = ch  # smallest letters to the earliest positions
        return "".join(out)
function smallestStringWithSwaps(s: string, pairs: number[][]): string {
    const parent = Array.from({ length: s.length }, (_, i) => i);

    const find = (x: number): number => {
        while (parent[x] !== x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    };

    for (const [a, b] of pairs) {
        parent[find(a)] = find(b);
    }
    const groups = new Map<number, number[]>();
    for (let i = 0; i < s.length; i++) {
        const root = find(i);
        if (!groups.has(root)) {
            groups.set(root, []);
        }
        groups.get(root)!.push(i);  // indices in increasing order
    }
    const out = [...s];
    for (const idx of groups.values()) {
        const letters = idx.map((i) => s[i]).sort();
        idx.forEach((i, t) => {
            out[i] = letters[t];  // smallest letters to the earliest positions
        });
    }
    return out.join("");
}
class Solution {
    private int[] parent;

    public String smallestStringWithSwaps(String s, List<List<Integer>> pairs) {
        parent = new int[s.length()];
        for (int i = 0; i < parent.length; i++) {
            parent[i] = i;
        }
        for (List<Integer> p : pairs) {
            parent[find(p.get(0))] = find(p.get(1));
        }
        Map<Integer, List<Integer>> groups = new HashMap<>();
        for (int i = 0; i < s.length(); i++) {
            groups.computeIfAbsent(find(i), k -> new ArrayList<>()).add(i);  // indices in increasing order
        }
        char[] out = s.toCharArray();
        for (List<Integer> idx : groups.values()) {
            char[] letters = new char[idx.size()];
            for (int t = 0; t < idx.size(); t++) {
                letters[t] = s.charAt(idx.get(t));
            }
            Arrays.sort(letters);
            for (int t = 0; t < idx.size(); t++) {
                out[idx.get(t)] = letters[t];  // smallest letters to the earliest positions
            }
        }
        return new String(out);
    }

    private int find(int x) {
        while (parent[x] != x) {
            parent[x] = parent[parent[x]];
            x = parent[x];
        }
        return x;
    }
}

What the code is doing, line by line:

  1. Repeated swaps along connected pairs can produce any permutation of a component.
  2. Sorted letters into sorted positions is the smallest arrangement of each component.

Dry run: use the Step through the solution player under the code. It runs this exact code on Example 1 and shows every line with the variables at that moment.

Edge cases to test:

  • No pairs (unchanged).
  • Everything connected (sorted string).
  • Repeated pairs.

Complexity: O(n log n + p α(n)) time, O(n) space.
